newsitem.title: USA: U.S. West Coast crude flat as refiners eye imports.
newsitem.headline: U.S. West Coast crude flat as refiners eye imports.

text.p: Spot trade for U.S. West Coast crudes was flat Tuesday, as refiners assessed demand for May and sought imports to replace pricey Alaska crude, traders said.

Alaska North Slope (ANS), which has been relatively high the last month, fell Monday on combination of weaker West Texas Intermediate (WTI) values and a wider discount after a cheaper-priced cargo sold.
Buyers were scarce, traders said, with talk that a major refiner in California was buying 1.5 million barrels of Ecuadorian crude (Oriente) through June.
ANS sold early yesterday at $1.02 off West Texas Intermediate (WTI), an 11-cent fall from the mid-March market price.
Despite Monday's ANS deal, major seller BP offered ANS at $0.90 under WTI.

Oriente's seller, Petroecuador, set term contract prices at -$2.56 off ANS last week and despite the losing price for lifters, traders, said West Coast would win cargoes at $1.00 off ANS, once transportation was included.
One trader said weak sour grade in the U.S. Gulf would encourage trading houses Glencore and Tripetrol to ship more Oriente to California.

In California markets, producers sold spot barrels of California Wilmington crude at 0.85 and 0.79 cents a barrels, traders said. The grade, used to make asphalt, edged up ahead of springtime demand for road repairs.
Other California grades were flat, with trade sapped the last week by the Easter holiday and scheduling on Line 63.
